subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on why the project might die [Thinking]
passage: Before writing a line of code, Lokesh's team of four sat on the terrace and did something odd. “It's April,” said Lakshmi. “The project is dead. Why?” They wrote fast on sticky notes: exams, nobody checked in, one person doing all the work, the thing got boring, someone lost the password. Lokesh read them out. Some were funny; some were uncomfortably true. Then they turned each note into a rule. Exam weeks went on the calendar as break weeks. Every part got two owners, not one. They chose a small showcase for the class on the last Friday of each month, so there would always be something to look forward to. The terrace felt lighter afterwards.

qa.q: What did the team imagine had happened to the project by April?
What might Lakshmi feel while listing the ways the project could die?
qa.a: A little uneasy but relieved: saying the risks aloud made them feel manageable.

qa.q: What else could the team do to spot trouble early, and why?
qa.a: Hold a short weekly check-in to notice when interest or work starts to slip, since trouble is easier to fix early.

qa.q: How does the plan look to a team member who feared doing all the work?
qa.a: Two owners for every part is a relief, since the load is no longer that person's alone.

grounding: Before starting, a team imagines the project dead in two months, lists the reasons and adds exam breaks and shared ownership.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on why the project might die [Thinking]
passage:
“Before we write a single line, try this,” Rehana said, pulling the laptop closer in the canteen. “It's two months from now. Our lost-and-found site is dead. Nobody updates it. Why?”
Harsha laughed. “Because it's us?”
“Seriously. Reasons.”
“Okay... unit tests in September. We all stop.”
“Good. Next.”
“Honestly? You'd end up doing everything, and when you get busy, it dies.”
Rehana winced, then typed it. “That's probably the real one. Third?”
“We get bored. It's not exciting after launch.”
“So: tests, one-person project, boredom.” She tapped the screen. “Tests are on the calendar, so we plan a two-week pause and tell people. For the one-person problem, each of us owns a section; you take the found-items page. Boredom... once a month we check if anyone's using it. If not, we fix it or stop honestly.”
Harsha nodded. “Okay. I'm in, for real this time.”

qa.q: Why did Rehana wince when Harsha named the second reason?
qa.a: Rehana felt a sting of recognition, since doing everything alone was probably the real risk, but was glad it was said aloud before starting.

qa.q: What else could the team add to the plan from this exercise?
qa.a: Keep the reasons and fixes where both can see them and revisit them at the monthly check, to see which risks are actually showing up.

qa.q: How might the plan feel to Harsha after this talk?
qa.a: Harsha has real ownership and a planned pause for tests, so joining feels safer and more serious, "for real this time".

grounding: Shows a team imagining its site abandoned in two months, naming exams, one person doing all the work and boredom, and planning around each.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on why the project might die [Thinking]
passage:
The best ten minutes of our project happened before we built anything. I'm Dhruv. Last year Leela and I, plus two others from the eco club, wanted a site where students could sign up to water the school garden.
It was August. Leela said, “Let's pretend it's October and the site is abandoned. Why did it die?” It felt gloomy, but we did it. We came up with three answers: half-yearly exams in September, only one of us knowing how to update it, and everyone losing interest once it stopped being new.
So we changed the plan on the spot. We marked the exam weeks on the calendar as a planned pause, with a notice on the site. All four of us learned to update the sign-up sheet, not just me. And we added a “garden of the month” photo to keep it fun.
It lasted until March. Not forever, but long past October.

qa.q: How many answers did the group come up with for why the site died?
How did Dhruv feel about Leela's exercise at first, and later?
qa.a: Dhruv found it gloomy at first, then felt relieved and a little proud, because naming the risks led to the planned pause and shared updating 😊

qa.q: Which other approach could the eco club have combined with this exercise?
qa.a: A monthly look at how many students signed up, so a slow decline would show early and could be fixed before the site died.

qa.q: How might Leela see the site lasting until March?
qa.a: Leela would likely feel the gloomy exercise was worth it, since the risks named that day were the ones they avoided.

grounding: Shows a team imagining its garden sign-up site abandoned two months later, naming exams, one-person upkeep and lost interest, and planning around them.
